papers.title: Progressive neurodegeneration of the locus coeruleus drives rapid eye movement sleep fragmentation
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common early features of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). AD progression is also characterized by early and substantial degeneration of the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC), beginning with tau pathology and progressing to major neuronal loss. Although LC degeneration and sleep disruption progress in parallel, whether LC degeneration causally contributes to sleep abnormalities, and which sleep changes are associated with this process, remain unresolved. Human studies are largely correlative, while existing rodent models poorly reproduce progressive LC degeneration. Here, we employed progressive Caspase-3 (Casp3)-mediated LC ablation, with longitudinal sleep and calcium fiber photometry to monitor LC activity across defined stages of degeneration in adult female DBH-Cre mice. Histological analysis demonstrated graded, time-dependent LC degeneration, yielding mild degeneration (~25% neuronal loss) by day 8 post Casp3 injection and moderate degeneration (~50% loss) by day 18. Relative to baseline and to control mice, LC degeneration led to REM sleep fragmentation, emerging already at the mild degeneration stage. By the moderate stage, total REM sleep during light hours had significantly increased, while EEG theta power during REM sleep progressively declined across all stages of degeneration. Degeneration also blunted state-dependent LC calcium activity, significantly reducing the contrast between wakefulness and REM signal. Together, these results establish Casp3-mediated ablation as a model of progressive LC neurodegeneration and identify REM fragmentation and blunted state-dependent LC activity as its early functional signatures, providing a platform for studying how degeneration of neuromodulatory systems shapes sleep in a neurodegenerative disease-like state.

papers.title: Between patterns and predictions: Interpretable latent EEG representations for clinical insights.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures rich brain dynamics, yet in clinical practice this complexity is often reduced to simplified summaries or categorical labels, limiting its interpretability for decision-making. We tested the hypothesis that a pretrained latent embedding framework, the Universal Map of EEG (UM-EEG), can preserve clinically meaningful structure across heterogeneous datasets and provide a generalizable representation of brain states. We applied UM-EEG, without retraining, to three independent cohorts spanning distinct clinical contexts: long-term EEG recordings from cardiac arrest patients (n = 575), subarachnoid hemorrhage (n = 100), and routine clinical EEG recordings containing physiological and pathological patterns (n = 141). EEG segments were projected into a 128-dimensional space anchored by expert-derived reference states, including wakefulness, sleep stages, ictal-interictal continuum activity, and burst suppression. Across datasets, favorable outcome or physiological recordings were consistently located closer to healthy reference states, whereas poor outcome and pathological recordings shifted toward pathological regions of the embedding space. Trajectory-derived geometric and temporal features discriminated outcome in cardiac arrest (ROC-AUC 0.83) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (ROC-AUC 0.76), and distinguished physiological from pathological routine EEGs (ROC-AUC 0.93). In routine EEG, similarity relationships derived from embedding trajectories correlated with those derived from structured clinical reports, indicating that the latent space recapitulates clinically relevant organization. These findings show that a fixed, semantically structured EEG embedding generalizes across etiologies and recording settings, enabling prognostic stratification and contextual interpretation while preserving the relational structure of brain states.

papers.title: Multichannel Polysomnographic Sensor Fusion for Automatic Sleep Stage Classification.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep stage classification can reduce the burden of manual polysomnographic scoring, but reliable models must account for heterogeneous physiological signals, temporal dependencies, and severe class imbalance. This study presents a dual-stream deep learning framework for five-class sleep staging from 30 s polysomnographic segments using two EEG signals, one EOG signal, and one submental EMG signal. Time-domain features are extracted through one-dimensional convolutions, while complementary time-frequency information is obtained from short-time Fourier transform spectrograms processed by a two-dimensional convolutional branch. The resulting features are fused and analyzed over a five-segment context window using a bidirectional long short-term memory network. Prolonged wake periods are censored only during training to reduce majority-class dominance without altering the evaluation distribution. Subject-wise five-fold cross-validation across 78 subjects yielded a mean accuracy of 91.5%, a balanced accuracy of 78.5%, a macro-F1 score of 77.4%, and a Cohen's kappa of 0.829. Controlled architectural and channel-ablation experiments further quantified the contributions of temporal context, time-frequency processing, wake censoring, and the individual PSG signals. A lightweight time-domain-only variant achieved 88.8% accuracy, 72.7% balanced accuracy, a macro-F1 score of 73.8%, and a Cohen's kappa of 0.779. These findings support the use of multimodal time-frequency fusion for robust automatic sleep staging while highlighting the trade-off between classification performance and model complexity.

papers.title: Modulating Sleep Oscillations Through Targeted Memory Reactivation: Linking Functional Dynamics to Brain Microstructure
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation reputedly rely on the coordinated activity of sleep oscillations, which may facilitate the reactivation and redistribution of newly acquired memories. Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during sleep can experimentally modulate these processes, although effects remain variable. Moreover, how learning-related microstructural plasticity relates to sleep oscillatory activity and spindle-related network dynamics remains poorly understood. We investigated whether auditory TMR modulates sleep spindles, slow oscillations (SOs) and their co-occurrence, whether these changes relate to motor memory consolidation and diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures of brain microstructure, and whether learning and TMR alter the evolution of cortico-cortical connectivity during spindle development. Methods: Sixty healthy young adults underwent five dMRI sessions before and after motor sequence learning (Day 1), after a post-training night of regular sleep (RS) or TMR (Day 2), and before and after relearning (Day 5). Baseline and experimental nights were recorded with 256-channel high-density EEG. Oscillation densities were analyzed using mixed-design ANOVAs and related to behavioral and dMRI changes using Pearson or Spearman correlations. Intra-spindle connectivity between 148 source-reconstructed cortical regions was compared between spindle onset and end, across nights and between groups using Network-Based Statistics. Results: Spindle density, SO density and SO-spindle co-occurrence remained stable across nights in the RS group but decreased after TMR. Higher spindle density and co-occurrence were associated with greater overnight performance gains, and all oscillatory measures were associated with learning-related dMRI changes in subcortical regions, notably striatum and thalamus. Connectivity increased from the beginning to the end of the spindle duration during the baseline night in both groups, but during the experimental night only in the RS group. Conclusions: Motor learning is associated with coordinated changes in sleep oscillatory activity, within-spindle cortical connectivity and brain microstructure, supporting a dynamic interaction between learning-induced plasticity and sleep-dependent network reorganization. Under the present stimulation conditions, TMR did not enhance these processes but instead reduced sleep oscillatory activity and attenuated spindle-related connectivity dynamics, underscoring the importance of precisely targeting endogenous sleep rhythms when using TMR.

Under the present stimulation conditions, TMR did not enhance motor memory consolidation but instead reduced sleep oscillatory activity and attenuated spindle-related connectivity dynamics.

papers.title: Molecular clockwork hypothesis for the KaiABC circadian oscillations.
papers.abstract: When three cyanobacterial proteins-KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC-are incubated with ATP in vitro, the phosphorylation level of KaiC exhibits stable circadian oscillations. Biochemical and structural analyses have shown that KaiC's ATPase activity is crucial for these oscillations, leading to the hypothesis that ATP-consuming dynamics function as a molecular clock, determining the oscillation period of individual molecules. Moreover, these molecular clocks synchronize collectively, resulting in oscillations at the ensemble level. In this study, we develop a theoretical model to test this molecular clockwork hypothesis. Our model clarifies the relationship between the oscillation period and ATPase activity, explaining the significant changes in the period induced by amino acid substitutions near the CI-CII domain boundary of the KaiC hexamer. Furthermore, the model addresses the physical basis for temperature compensation concerning both the oscillation period and ATPase activity. Thus, the molecular clockwork perspective provides a framework for understanding the atomic design behind collective oscillations.

papers.title: Vigilance profiles at sleep onset in patients with difficulty initiating sleep, with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: Difficulty initiating sleep (DIS) is a core insomnia complaint, frequently associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms, yet its objective correlates remain elusive. Insomnia subtypes were merged into a single diagnosis in DSM-5 and ICSD-3 because their criteria lacked reliability, leaving open whether objective markers could help characterize insomnia heterogeneity. Conventional polysomnography (PSG) reduces the wake-sleep transition to a single 30-s epoch. We combined conventional and continuous EEG-based vigilance markers to characterize sleep onset in patients with and without a DIS complaint, and in patients with DIS with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed PSG recordings from 2,952 sleep-clinic patients, grouped by the self-reported complaint of difficulty falling asleep (Insomnia Severity Index item 1 [≥] 2: DIS, n = 1,328; no DIS, n = 1,624). In unmedicated patients with DIS (n = 556), depressive (BDI-II [≥] 14) and anxiety (STAI-T [≥] 45) symptoms were assessed. Vigilance was quantified on 3-s epochs with an intrinsic Vigilance Score (iVS), a probability-of-wakefulness index calibrated on each participant's own scored night, alongside the theta/alpha ratio and micro-sleep detection, and on 30-s epochs with automated hypnodensities. Results: Patients with DIS showed a longer sleep latency and slightly higher vigilance markers during both wakefulness and sleep, whereas the duration of the SOP itself was only marginally different (median 11.5 min in both groups). Deep sleep also accumulated later across the night (hypnodensity). In wakefulness preceding sleep onset, higher vigilance coexisted with more frequent brief vigilance drops. Among patients with DIS, depressive symptoms were associated with a less wake-like sleep-onset period despite more severe insomnia complaints, a finding not explained by differences in wake amount and convergent with hypnodensity. Anxiety symptoms showed a similar but weaker, non-significant pattern. Conclusions: In patients complaining of difficulty initiating sleep, the delay lies mainly before the first sleep epoch: once it is reached, progression to consolidated sleep is only marginally delayed, although its vigilance content may differ. Continuous EEG markers detect such differences, which are not captured by sleep staging. The association of depressive symptoms with a less vigilant sleep onset, despite worse complaints, suggests that similar insomnia complaints may rest on partly different physiological substrates, and that continuous vigilance markers could help revisit insomnia heterogeneity.

papers.title: Circadian system and human health: From molecular mechanisms to clinical integration.
papers.abstract: The circadian system, an evolutionarily conserved endogenous oscillator coordinating physiological adaptation to geophysical cycles, coordinates hierarchical gene regulatory networks, metabolic pathways, and physiological functions to maintain organismal homeostasis. Circadian disturbances caused by modern lifestyle are recognized as key etiological factors in complex multisystem disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic, and oncogenic pathologies. The review synthesizes current evidence to delineate that organ-specific physiological programs across the human body are under circadian clock, and chronic desynchronization of system drives a broad spectrum of clinical disorders. Moreover, the review critically assesses state-of-the-art therapeutic modalities, and identifies promising technological innovations. It advances precision chronomedicine by proposing public health interventions, such as environmental modification combined with behavioral education, offering a roadmap for clinical implementation of circadian restoration therapies.

papers.title: Tracking Vigilance While Driving: Pilot Study of Heart Rate Variability Classification Under a Controlled Sleep-Deprivation Protocol.
papers.abstract: Decreased vigilance associated with drowsiness is a major cause of motor vehicle crashes, but its physiological characterization and detection remain difficult due to behavioral and environmental confounding factors. This study presents an original experimental framework combining a highly controlled sleep-deprivation protocol, repeated driving simulations, and a machine-learning-based heart rate variability (HRV) analysis to study the physiological and behavioral changes in vigilance during a prolonged period of wakefulness while driving. Twelve healthy young adults participated in a 30-h sleep-deprivation constant routine protocol that included driving simulations every two hours, with data collection: electrocardiography (ECG), subjective ratings of drowsiness, psychomotor vigilance test, and driving performance. The collected data was separated into two clearly identifiable vigilance states, a "Rested" and a "Tired" state, respectively, for the first and last driving sessions, of the protocol. Heart rate variability (HRV) features were extracted from ECG recordings, statistically analyzed, and submitted into supervised machine learning classifiers using participant-independent validation to assess their ability to distinguish between two experimentally defined states of vigilance. The accuracy of state separation was verified based on significant alterations observed in drowsiness ratings and psychomotor performance in the Tired compared to the Rested state. The variability in driving behavior, an indicator of impaired driving ability, increased significantly from the Rested compared to the Tired state. Several HRV features revealed significant differences between Rested and Tired states, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large, observed for several metrics. Participant-independent machine learning analysis, namely Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSO-CV), showed that HRV metrics enable reliable discrimination between vigilance states, with all classifiers evaluated achieving average accuracy greater than 85%. This pilot study demonstrated that the proposed experimental framework, by reducing the major behavioral and environmental confounding factors, can generate two distinct states of vigilance at the physiological and behavioral levels, enabling reliable separation of experimental data, independent of any additional ground truths. The states separated by the framework enable the detection of decreased driving performance and efficiently label HRV data for vigilance classification. Nevertheless, the findings should be interpreted within the context of a pilot study conducted with a small cohort of healthy young adults.

papers.title: An Interpretable Framework for Identifying EEG Spectral Biomarkers of Pathological Brain Aging.
papers.abstract: Background: Normal aging involves gradual declines in brain function, whereas neurodegenerative disorders show accelerated deterioration. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures alterations in brain oscillatory activity, making it promising for detecting neurodegenerative disorders. However, existing approaches often emphasize classification performance over spectral biomarker identification, limiting clinical translation. Methods: We propose an EEG-based framework integrating explainable machine learning, analyses of inter-subject heterogeneity and temporal stability, and probabilistic modeling to identify reproducible spectral biomarkers of pathological brain aging. Two independent public EEG datasets comprising cognitively normal (CN) individuals and patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) were analyzed. Spectral features from canonical frequency bands were analyzed using SHAP to identify reproducible biomarkers in two datasets. The identified biomarker was subsequently characterized through inter-subject heterogeneity, temporal stability, and empirical distributions to assess disease-related alterations in oscillatory activity. Results: Several spectral features showed consistent disease-related associations across classification tasks. The θ/α ratio emerged as a representative biomarker, showing reduced temporal stability and broader empirical distributions in most neurodegenerative groups than in CN. Conclusions: Reduced temporal stability of reproducible EEG spectral biomarkers may represent an observable signature of disrupted oscillatory brain organization during pathological aging. The proposed framework characterizes a dimension of EEG spectral biomarkers that static summaries discard, offering an interpretable basis on which future longitudinal studies may build diagnostic and monitoring tools.

papers.title: Clockophagy in Alzheimer's Disease: An Emerging Hypothesis Linking Circadian Dysfunction to Ferroptotic Vulnerability.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is frequently associated with sleep disturbances and circadian dysfunction, which may precede or accompany clinical manifestations and have been associated with amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology, tau abnormalities, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal vulnerability. Increasing evidence suggests that circadian regulation intersects with multiple cellular processes implicated in AD pathogenesis, including autophagy and ferroptosis. Among these mechanisms, clockophagy, an SQSTM1/p62-mediated selective autophagic process involved in BMAL1 degradation, has recently emerged as a potential molecular link between circadian regulation and cellular stress responses. In this review, we summarize current evidence connecting sleep disruption, circadian dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptotic susceptibility in AD, while highlighting the current limitations of mechanistic evidence. We further discuss the molecular basis of clockophagy and its potential relationship with BMAL1 regulation, oxidative lipid damage, and ferroptosis. Collectively, clockophagy is currently viewed as an emerging hypothesis that may contribute to AD-related pathological processes. Finally, we discuss potential therapeutic implications, including approaches targeting sleep and circadian organization, BMAL1-associated regulatory pathways, and lipid oxidative stress. Further studies are required to determine whether modulation of clockophagy can influence AD-related neurodegenerative processes.

papers.title: Frequent involvement of cingulate and insulo-opercular regions in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy: A multimodal presurgical study.
papers.abstract: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is classically considered a frontal lobe epilepsy; however, accumulating evidence suggests that hypermotor seizures may arise from multiple frontal and extrafrontal regions. We characterized the anatomical distribution of best available localizations in patients with SHE using multimodal presurgical data. We retrospectively analyzed 17 patients with clinically diagnosed SHE who underwent comprehensive evaluation, including long-term video-electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, 3-T high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and, where indicated, magnetoencephalography, stereo-EEG (SEEG), and surgical assessment. Best available anatomical localizations were assigned using a hierarchical multimodal framework incorporating surgical, SEEG, and concordant noninvasive findings. Their anatomical distribution was subsequently assessed at the cohort level. Sixteen patients (94.1%) had an assigned best available localization. Cingulate or insulo-opercular regions were involved in 11 of 16 patients (68.8%), whereas the remaining cases were localized to other frontal regions. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 10 patients with SEEG-defined and/or surgically supported localizations, six involved cingulate or insulo-opercular regions. All patients were MRI-negative. In contrast, MRI-positron emission tomography fusion provided regionally informative anatomical findings in 16 of 17 cases and contributed to multimodal localization. Interictal epileptiform discharges were identified in 15 patients, whereas regionally informative ictal scalp EEG patterns were observed in eight; ictal interpretation was frequently limited by rapid propagation, movement-related artifacts, and delayed EEG onset. Focal cortical dysplasia-related histopathological findings were identified in five of seven resected specimens, whereas interpretation in two was limited by prior thermocoagulation. These descriptive findings indicate that cingulate and insulo-opercular regions were frequently represented among the identified localizations in this presurgical cohort. Multimodal evaluation integrating electroclinical, imaging, and invasive findings may support presurgical localization in MRI-negative SHE.

papers.title: An Efficient Convolutional Neural Network Model for Classifying Positive Affective States from EEG Data Considering Sleep Condition.
papers.abstract: The recognition of affective states from EEG recordings considering the sleep condition can be an important supporting tool in therapy and in the treatment of psychological or psychiatric disorders. Since sleep deprivation changes EEG characteristics, a two-stage framework is developed for affective state classification. First, a classification between "Normal Sleep" (NS) and "Sleep-Deprived" (SD) is conducted using resting-state EEG data. The data are then fed into one of two newly proposed, lightweight Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to recognize four affective states. In the first stage, CNN-BiLSTM achieves 95.96% accuracy under window-level splitting and 70.46% under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation, while in the second stage the proposed models achieve 93.40% (NS) and 90.95% (SD) under window-level splitting, and 38.98% (NS) and 38.97% (SD) under cross-validation. The lower subject-independent accuracies reflect the class imbalance and the clustering of scores near the class boundaries, which make cross-subject four-class generalization challenging. As existing studies mostly classify momentary emotions without addressing sleep conditions, direct comparison with prior work is difficult; we therefore benchmarked our framework against several established baseline models, including SqueezeNet, EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest. This study suggests that considering physiological states can improve multi-class classification of affective states from time-varying neurophysiological signals such as EEG. The framework performs strongly under window-level evaluation, whereas its performance under the stricter subject-independent setting is more limited and should be interpreted accordingly. It can nonetheless contribute to more comprehensive research in affective neuroscience.

papers.title: Is cardiovascular autonomic control during the day-to-night transition dependent on dim light melatonin onset? An exploratory analysis in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: We tested whether dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) is time-aligned with the transition between biological day into night in cardiovascular autonomic control (CV onset time). We studied 10 healthy adults (4 females, age 25 ± SD 2 years) under an ultra-short semi-constant routine protocol (<8lux). Participants remained seated for 7 h until 1 h after their habitual bedtime. We collected saliva samples every 30 min and recorded R-R intervals and beat-to-beat blood pressure every hour. DLMO was defined as the interpolated time for melatonin increase over 3 pg/mL. Phase angle was defined as the time difference between DLMO and the midpoint of self-reported sleep as a measure of the alignment between sleep-wake patterns and biological circadian rhythms. CV onset time was defined using a segmental (piecewise) analysis to identify the inflection point (X0 slope) throughout the study. CV autonomic modulation was assessed using indices of heart rate and blood pressure variability. CV onset times for all indices did not differ significantly from DLMO (p > 0.05). Mean differences between DLMO and CV onset time were significantly correlated with the phase angle of entrainment (all significant, r > +0.75). Our results suggest that CV autonomic transition into biological night was not associated with DLMO, which seems to depend on the phase angle of entrainment.

papers.title: Salivary Dim-Light Melatonin Onset is Associated with Functional Decline, Respiratory Symptom Emergence, and Survival in Early Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake and circadian disturbances are increasingly recognized in people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (plwALS), but endogenous circadian phase timing and its prognostic significance in early disease remain unclear. We assessed whether salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), an objective marker of central circadian phase, is altered in early plwALS and whether it provides prognostic information. In this prospective longitudinal observational study, plwALS within 18 months of symptom onset underwent home-based salivary melatonin sampling under dim-light conditions at 6 predefined time points around habitual sleep onset. Melatonin profiles were modeled using cubic smoothing splines, and DLMO was defined when the fitted curve first reached 3 pg/ml. Clinical, respiratory, and sleep assessments were collected at baseline (T0) and after 6 months (T6); a subgroup repeated saliva sampling at T6. Age- and sex-matched controls underwent melatonin profiling. Associations with disease progression, incident respiratory symptoms, and survival/tracheostomy were examined using regressions and survival analyses. A total of 50 plwALS were enrolled. Compared with controls, plwALS showed an earlier DLMO (20:24 ± 1:18 vs 20:58 ± 0:50; p = 0.028) despite similar habitual sleep onset and chronotype. Within ALS cohort, a later baseline DLMO correlated with worse functional/motor status, faster progression of disease, incident dyspnea/orthopnea by T6 (adjusted OR 3.11; p = 0.019), and poorer survival/tracheostomy-free outcome. In the resampled subgroup (n = 28), DLMO and melatonin-derived metrics did not change over ~6 months. Circadian phase alterations are detectable in early ALS. Baseline DLMO showed exploratory associations with functional, respiratory, and survival outcomes. Larger independent cohorts are required before DLMO can be considered a validated prognostic biomarker. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: Neuroelectrophysiological correlates of extended cessation of consciousness in advanced meditators: A multimodal EEG and MEG study
papers.abstract: In some contemplative traditions, 'extended cessation' (EC) refers to a state of advanced meditation in which the meditator self-reports intentionally suppressing their own consciousness and re-emerging with a profound sense of clarity and equanimity. Here, we present the first electrophysiological study of EC, in which five meditators underwent concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recording. EC significantly increased high-frequency global coherence in all five of the participants, yet it did not consistently affect Lempel-Ziv complexity or power across participants. Our results provide preliminary evidence that the neural signatures of EC may be distinct from other states that are characterized by a loss of consciousness, including deep sleep and anesthesia. EC may not be simply 'switching off' consciousness but rather reorganizing the neural dynamics that underlie consciousness.

papers.title: Emotional Processing in a Nap Paradigm: The Role of Sleep Stages in Memory and Reactivity.
papers.abstract: It is widely known that sleep has a role in modulating emotional processing. However, while sleep facilitates the consolidation of emotional memories, its influence on emotional reactivity remains unclear. Most prior work has not fully addressed emotional reactivity, often relying solely on subjective or physiological measures, nor has it disentangled the contribution of different sleep stages. Here, using a between-subjects design, we asked participants to complete two picture-based tasks assessing emotional memory and emotional reactivity before and after a manipulation condition (nap, N = 40; wake, N = 40), and again 2 days later. Spontaneous variations in nap duration resulted in participants reaching REM sleep (REM group, N = 20) or not (No-REM group, N = 20). Emotional reactivity, assessed using an emotional picture task consisting of 28 images with different emotional contents (negative and neutral), was measured through subjective ratings and physiological responses (phasic cardiac response and skin conductance response). Sleep preserved memory performance relative to wakefulness, but after 2 days, only negative images maintained a memory advantage in the Nap group; however, no differences emerged as a function of REM sleep occurrence during the nap. For emotional reactivity, subjective arousal decreased after sleep in the REM group, whereas valence ratings declined only after 2 days. Physiologically, heart rate habituation was greater in the No-REM group. Together, these findings indicate that sleep fosters emotional memory consolidation while modulating reactivity in ways that diverge across subjective and physiological domains, with a decrease in subjective arousal ratings and an increase in phasic cardiac response. These findings, which should be interpreted in the context of the observed differences in participants' sleep architecture, highlight the complex role of sleep in emotional processing and underscore the need for standardized experimental paradigms.

papers.title: Video EEG in pediatric epilepsy: Diagnostic significance and association between frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to compare video electroencephalogram (VEEG) and routine electroencephalogram (EEG) in childhood epilepsy diagnosis and analyze the correlation between EEG frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity. One hundred and sixty children suspected of having epilepsy underwent routine EEG and VEEG examinations. Diagnostic efficacy and detection rates were compared. Cognitive function was evaluated in 80 children diagnosed with epilepsy, who were allocated into normal intelligence (35 cases), borderline intelligence (25 cases), and intelligence-impaired (20 cases) groups. Clinical data, EEG parameters, and their correlation with cognitive impairment were analyzed. VEEG showed higher sensitivity, accuracy, and negative predictive value, and detection rates of epileptiform discharges, synchronous clinical seizures, and clinical symptoms than routine EEG (p < 0.05). Clinical characteristics and EEG parameters differed among the three groups (p < 0.05). The relative power of δ and θ bands and the awake and sleep discharge indices were positively correlated with cognitive impairment severity (r = 0.300, 0.643, 0.622, and 0.456), whereas α and β band power were negatively correlated (r = -0.515 and -0.410) (all p < 0.001). VEEG demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than routine EEG, and EEG frequency band power was correlated with cognitive impairment severity.

papers.title: Cognitive tests of pattern separation as sleep-sensitive measures in middle-aged and older adults: An exploratory study
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are considered both a dementia risk factor and symptom. The present research aimed to identify cognitive tests sensitive to objective sleep quantity or quality, focusing on tests designed to evaluate the earliest cognitive changes in dementia. We recruited adults who were 50 years or older and remotely monitored their sleep patterns for 7 consecutive days using wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries. On day 7, participants completed different cognitive tests; the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), the Prodromal Alzheimers and Mild Cognitive Impairment battery from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), taxing pattern separation, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The final sample included 34 participants (mean age: 65.56, SD: 9.57). There were significant correlations between objective sleep quantity and PVT and MST performance. MoCA scores were correlated with performance on CANTAB and MST. Objective sleep quantity predicted MST performance when controlling for age, sex, and education. Tests of pattern separation are sensitive to objective sleep quantity and early cognitive changes associated with dementia. The sensitivity of pattern separation tests to sleep should be evaluated in a larger study, aiming to identify suitable clinical trial outcome measures for sleep-promoting treatments in older adults.

papers.title: Circadian Misalignment and Chrononutrition in Type 2 Diabetes: Mechanistic Insights and Translational Gaps.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate glucose metabolism, insulin secretion, hepatic glucose production, peripheral insulin sensitivity, nutrient handling, and energy balance. Observational studies have associated circadian timing disruption through shift work, irregular sleep, artificial light at night, social jet lag, late eating, or inconsistent meal timing with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This narrative review integrates molecular, clinical, nutritional, and pharmacological evidence linking circadian misalignment with diabetes, with emphasis on chrononutrition, time-restricted eating, glucose variability, diabetes-related complications, melatonin/MTNR1B-related susceptibility, exogenous melatonin, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), digital phenotyping, and chronopharmacology. A structured narrative literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies on circadian biology, diabetes, meal timing, time-restricted eating, melatonin signaling, MTNR1B, circadian biomarkers, CGM, and time-informed therapeutic strategies. Mechanistic and preclinical studies establish clock-metabolism coupling, whereas controlled human physiological studies support time-of-day variation in insulin secretion, postprandial responses, and glucose handling; diabetes-specific interventional and complication-outcome evidence remains limited. Chrononutrition and time-restricted eating may support glycemic regulation only as individualized adjuncts to standard diabetes care, not as replacements for established treatment; medication review and hypoglycemia monitoring are essential, particularly for patients using insulin or insulin secretagogues. Translation into routine care requires longer diabetes-specific trials, standardized outcomes, validated biomarkers, and patient-centered implementation protocols.

papers.title: Race-ethnic minoritized veterans diagnosed with sleep apnea, insomnia, and COMISA at the Veterans Health Administration have lower all-cause mortality than Non-Hispanic White veterans.
papers.abstract: Few data exist exploring the relationship between sleep apnea (SA), insomnia, comorbid insomnia and sleep apnea (COMISA) and mortality among race-ethnic minoritized (REM) US veterans. This study compares all-cause mortality among Veterans Health Administration (VHA) patients diagnosed with these sleep disorders by race-ethnicity. The study included veterans with confirmed diagnoses and prescribed treatment for insomnia and/or SA, within the VHA, from 1999 to 2023. Using self-reported data, eight race-ethnicity groups were generated (i.e., Non-Hispanic White [NH-W], Non-Hispanic Black [NH-B], Hispanic White [H-W], Hispanic Black [H-B], Non-Hispanic Asian [NH-A], Non-Hispanic American Indian/Alaska Native [NH-AIAN], Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander [NH-NHPI]). Sleep diagnoses required International Classification of Diseases documentation. Additionally, insomnia was defined in those prescribed sleep medication or CBT-I while SA was defined in those prescribed positive airway pressure (PAP). All-cause mortality was extracted from national databases. For each sleep disorder, multivariable logistic regression determined the association between race-ethnicity and all-cause mortality, using NH-W as reference. Models were adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, medications, exposure time, and neighborhood socioeconomics. This cohort consisted of 1,544,541 veterans (70% NH-W, 20% NH-B, 6.0% H-W, 1.2% NH-A, and 0.9% NH-AIAN). In adjusted analyses, compared to NH-Ws, REM veterans had lower mortality in SA (NH-A OR 0.30 [95% CI 0.27-0.33]; NH-NHPI OR 0.79 [95% CI 0.74-0.85], insomnia (NH-A OR 0.34 [95% CI 0.31-0.37]; NH-NHPI OR 0.84 [95% CI 0.74-0.86], and COMISA (NH-A OR 0.28 [95% CI 0.23-0.35]; NH-AIAN OR 0.71 [95% CI 0.61-0.83]. These data suggest that REM veterans using VHA sleep care have lower sleep disorder-related all-cause mortality than NH-White veterans, suggesting attenuated racial-ethnic mortality disparities within this equal-access healthcare setting.

papers.title: Fear-EEG-AI: A Conceptual and Operational Framework for Designing EEG-AI Systems for the Inference of Fear-Compatible Neurophysiological States.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and artificial intelligence (AI) are central tools in affective computing, yet fear-related inference remains constrained by a gap between experimental performance and deployable evidence: high accuracy on controlled datasets guarantees neither neurobiological specificity, nor robustness across users, nor traceable inference. EEG does not measure fear directly; it captures cortical dynamics compatible with threat processing, arousal or vigilance. This paper introduces the Fear-EEG-AIFramework, a technology-independent architecture for designing, validating and deploying EEG-AI systems targeting fear-compatible neurophysiological states. Building on a prior systematic review, it organizes development into three hierarchical levels-neurobiological foundation, neuroelectric correlates and computational modeling-governed by six cross-cutting principles, and makes them evaluable through eight observable dimensions, the Fear-EEG-AI Alignment Index (FAI) and five validation evidence levels. Applied to the eight eligible studies of that corpus by two raters who had not drafted the instrument, with adjudication by a third, the rubric reached 67.2% exact agreement (quadratic-weighted κ=0.741; ICC(2,1) =0.744). Under 10,000 admissible weightings the equal-weight ordering survived in 10.1% of draws, and one of 56 ordered pairs met a stability criterion fixed before the pairwise results were tabulated. The index is therefore reported as a descriptor of methodological documentation and not as a ranking of implementations.

papers.title: CSTO-Net: Cross-View Spectral-Transport and Topology-Operator Network for EEG Emotion Recognition.
papers.abstract: Multi-view electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition must decide how the spectral graph sets of different connectivity views correspond and how their graph propagation operators interact. We present CSTO-Net, a cross-view spectral-transport and topology-operator network for EEG-based emotion recognition.Approach: CSTO-Net integrates three window-wise views: dynamic differential entropy (DDE) as node attributes, amplitude-envelope Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) graphs, and phase-locking value (PLV) graphs. Cross-View Spectral Transport Routing (CSTR) formulates PCC-PLV spectral correspondence as an entropy-regularized optimal-transport problem with explicit marginal constraints, deliberately separating correspondence estimation from band-importance estimation. Directional Cross-Topology Modulation (DCTM) performs ordered composition of the two routed propagation operators on shared node features and encodes order-dependent propagation discrepancy via a provably skew-symmetric graph-operator commutator with signed decomposition.Main results: On the Database for Emotion Analysis using Physiological Signals (DEAP) dataset, CSTO-Net achieves 93.95 ± 2.50% valence and 94.97 ± 2.72% arousal accuracy under the subject-dependent setting, and 93.73% and 94.54% under participant-wise five-fold subject-independent cross-validation across 32 participants. On the SJTU Emotion EEG Dataset (SEED), it achieves 93.12% under the standard subject-dependent split, 91.36% under 15-fold leave-one-subject-out evaluation across 15 participants, and 98.05 ± 2.32% under subject-dependent five-fold cross-validation. Ablation studies confirm that both CSTR and DCTM contribute substantially to recognition accuracy.Significance: These results demonstrate that explicit cross-view spectral correspondence and topology-operator-level interaction provide complementary benefits for EEG emotion recognition, offering an interpretable route for modeling order-sensitive interactions between functional connectivity views.

papers.title: Association between low-carbohydrate diet scores and macrovascular events or all-cause mortality in adults with type 1 diabetes in Japan.
papers.abstract: The effects of lifestyle factors on macrovascular events or all-cause mortality remain unclear in type 1 diabetes. We examined the associations of diet, physical activity, and sleep with these outcomes among adults with type 1 diabetes living in Japan. This multicenter prospective cohort included 352 adults with type 1 diabetes from the Juntendo-Aso Type 1 Diabetes cohort. Lifestyle factors were assessed by questionnaire. Dietary intake was evaluated using a brief-type self-administered diet history questionnaire, from which Total, Plant, and Animal low-carbohydrate diet scores were calculated. The primary composite outcome was the first occurrence of ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral artery disease, or all-cause mortality. Associations were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models. Mean age was 51.4 ± 15.1 years, mean HbA1c was 7.9 ± 1.1%, and carbohydrate accounted for 49.3% of energy intake. During follow-up, 35 participants experienced the primary composite outcome. In multivariable Cox models, the Total LCDS (HR, 0.90; 95% CI: 0.82-0.98; P = 0.012), Plant LCDS (HR, 0.85; 95% CI: 0.76-0.94; P = 0.003), and Animal LCDS (HR, 0.93; 95% CI: 0.87-0.996; P = 0.037) were inversely associated with the outcome. Among adults with type 1 diabetes living in Japan, low-carbohydrate dietary patterns, particularly the Plant low-carbohydrate diet score, were inversely associated with macrovascular events or all-cause mortality.

papers.title: Whole-Room Indirect Calorimetry in the Study of Obesity, Insulin Resistance and Metabolic Flexibility: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Obesity and insulin resistance are characterized by substantial heterogeneity in energy expenditure and substrate utilization. Whole-room indirect calorimetry (WRIC) enables continuous assessment of oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, energy expenditure, respiratory exchange ratio (RER), and substrate oxidation under controlled conditions. This narrative review examines the physiological interpretation, methodological strengths, limitations, and applications of WRIC in obesity, insulin resistance, metabolic flexibility, and weight-loss interventions. By enabling prolonged observation during resting, postprandial, exercise, and sleep periods, WRIC complements short-term indirect calorimetry and free-living energy expenditure measurements obtained using doubly labeled water. Validation studies generally demonstrate high technical accuracy and reproducibility for respiratory gas exchange and 24 h energy expenditure measured using WRIC. In contrast, estimates of the thermic effect of food, short-term changes in RER, and substrate oxidation are more sensitive to protocol design, energy balance, physical activity, and analytical procedures. Available studies demonstrate substantial interindividual variability rather than a uniform metabolic pattern associated with obesity or insulin resistance. Direct WRIC evidence concerning contemporary anti-obesity pharmacotherapy and metabolic and bariatric surgery remains limited. Standardized protocols and complementary assessments of body composition, insulin sensitivity, and free-living energy expenditure are needed to improve the comparability and interpretation of findings across studies.

papers.title: Nutrition, Circadian Regulation, and the Gut-Melatonin-Visceral Adipose Tissue Axis: An Integrative Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) dysfunction is a major determinant of obesity-related metabolic disorders, including insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Growing evidence indicates that VAT function is regulated by a complex interplay between nutrition, circadian rhythms, intestinal melatonin secretion, and the gut microbiota rather than by isolated metabolic pathways. The gastrointestinal tract represents an important interface between dietary exposures, microbial activity, immune signaling, and host metabolic regulation. Melatonin is a potential component of this network because it participates in circadian regulation and has been detected in gastrointestinal tissues, while experimental studies suggest that intestinal melatonin signaling may interact with gut microbial and metabolic processes. However, the cellular sources, quantitative contribution, local dynamics, and physiological significance of intestinal melatonin remain incompletely established, particularly in humans. This narrative review integrates current evidence regarding the interactions between nutrition, circadian regulation, intestinal melatonin, gut microbiota, and visceral adipose tissue. Rather than proposing a validated causal pathway, we introduce the Gut-Melatonin-Visceral Adipose Tissue (Gut-Melatonin-VAT) Axis as an integrative, hypothesis-generating conceptual framework that organizes established interactions together with candidate mechanisms requiring further experimental validation. Particular attention is given to the bidirectional relationships among dietary composition, meal timing, microbial rhythmicity, intestinal signaling, immune regulation, and VAT dysfunction. The framework may provide a basis for generating testable hypotheses concerning nutritional, chrononutritional, microbiota-targeted, and melatonin-related interventions, while recognizing that direct human evidence validating the complete pathway is currently lacking.

papers.title: Beyond the Apnea-Hypopnea Index: Cardiovascular and Metabolic Phenotyping of Hypertensive Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is strongly associated with hypertension, yet the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), while it defines the presence and frequency of respiratory events, predicts cardiovascular risk less reliably in the individual patient than metrics that incorporate the depth and duration of hypoxic exposure. Patients with comparable AHI values can differ substantially in nocturnal hypoxemia, sympathetic activation, ambulatory blood pressure behavior, and target-organ damage, exposing a persistent gap between respiratory classification and cardiovascular prognosis. This review synthesizes current evidence on the mechanisms linking OSA to hypertension, intermittent hypoxia, chemoreflex-mediated sympathetic overactivity, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation, hypoxia-associated insulin resistance and examines emerging metrics, including hypoxic burden, oxygen desaturation index, and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, that capture cardiovascular risk more accurately than AHI alone. We describe six cardiovascular phenotypes of hypertension in OSA: resistant, nocturnal, non-dipping/reverse-dipping, masked, and morning-surge hypertension, alongside hypertension-mediated target-organ damage, each with distinct mechanisms, prognosis, and treatment response. Because intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic activation are also implicated in insulin resistance and MASLD, this shared metabolic pathway is integrated throughout rather than treated as an incidental comorbidity. Building on this evidence, we propose a phenotype-oriented clinical framework spanning cardiovascular screening, multidomain phenotyping, risk stratification, and personalized therapy intended to complement, not replace, AHI-based diagnosis and current hypertension guidelines. This framework is presented as a conceptual, expert-derived proposal intended to structure clinical reasoning, and it has not been derived from or validated in an independent cohort. We conclude with future directions, including digital biomarkers, multimodal imaging, and artificial intelligence-assisted phenotyping, as pathways toward precision cardiovascular medicine in hypertensive patients with OSA.

papers.title: The effects of multiregional fascial mobilization on heart rate and physiological parameters in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with increased sympathetic activity and an elevated cardiovascular risk. Noninvasive interventions targeting autonomic regulation may offer complementary therapeutic strategies. This randomized controlled trial aimed to investigate the acute effects of multiregional fascial mobilization on the physiological parameters of patients with OSA. Patients with polysomnography-confirmed moderate-to-severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥ 15 events/hour) were randomly assigned to an intervention group that received a standardized 16-minute multiregional fascial mobilization protocol or a control group that rested quietly in the supine position for the corresponding period without receiving manual or tactile intervention. The intervention targeted the cervical, thoracic, and abdominal regions, under controlled conditions. The primary outcomes included heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and peripheral oxygen saturation. Measurements were obtained at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and 5 and 15 minutes post-intervention. A total of 95 male patients (mean age: 48.12 ± 10.21 years) completed the study. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups, except for heart rate. After adjustment for baseline heart rate using mixed analysis of covariance, no significant group × time interaction was observed for heart rate (P = .476, partial ηp2 = .008). Similarly, no significant group × time interactions were observed for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, or peripheral oxygen saturation (all P > .05). Although significant time effects were observed for some physiological parameters, the magnitude of these effects varied across outcomes, and none was accompanied by a significant group × time interaction. Therefore, these temporal changes were not interpreted as intervention-specific effects. No adverse events were reported. Heart rate changed significantly over time following the interventions; however, after adjustment for baseline heart rate, the pattern of change did not differ significantly between the fascial mobilization and control groups. Similarly, no significant between-group differences in changes over time were observed for blood pressure or oxygen saturation. These findings do not demonstrate a specific acute effect of multiregional fascial mobilization on the physiological parameters assessed. Further studies using advanced measures of autonomic function and longer follow-up periods are warranted.

papers.title: The Core Circadian Clock Gene PiLUX, a MYB-Family Transcription Factor, Enhances Cold Tolerance in Plumbago indica L.
papers.abstract: Low-temperature stress is a key environmental factor limiting the introduction and cultivation of plants native to tropical and subtropical regions; however, the molecular mechanisms governing their cold tolerance are not fully understood. In this study, we identified a core circadian rhythm gene-PiLUX-in the ornamental and medicinal plant Plumbago indica L. (P. indica) and systematically analyzed its role in the plant's response to low temperatures. Transcriptomic analysis and physiological measurements indicated that PiLUX is significantly upregulated following cold induction; furthermore, its transcriptional levels show positive correlations with cold-tolerance-related physiological indicators such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging capacity, osmoregulatory substance accumulation, and membrane lipid peroxidation. In transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana (A. thaliana), heterologous overexpression of PiLUX enhances cold tolerance but also delays flowering, suggesting that reproductive development is sacrificed to conserve nutrients for cold tolerance. VIGS experiments confirmed that PiLUX knockdown exacerbates oxidative damage in P. indica under cold stress and reduces its recovery ability. The experimental results and transcriptomic data suggest that PiLUX may participate in the low-temperature response downstream of, or in parallel with, the CBF pathway; however, direct regulatory evidence is still required. This study provides insights into the adaptation strategies of thermophilic plants under low-temperature stress and offers a theoretical basis and genetic resources for cold-tolerance breeding in P. indica.

papers.title: Prevalence of meeting sleep duration recommendations among over 1.4 million children and adolescents across 58 countries: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the prevalence of children and adolescents meeting sleep duration recommendations across international studies and to examine variation by age group, day type, sex, and region. Three databases were searched. Eligible studies reported adherence to age-specific recommendations (9-11 h/day for children and 8-10 h/day for adolescents). Subjective or proxy-reported estimates were pooled using maximum-likelihood random-effects models of logit-transformed proportions with Knapp-Hartung confidence intervals. Fifty-three studies including 1,402,868 participants (49.7% female) were included. Pooled prevalence was 76.5% (95% CI 71.6-80.9) in children and 54.8% (95% CI 50.0-59.6) in adolescents. Adolescents had lower odds of meeting recommendations before multiplicity adjustment (OR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.15-0.94; p = 0.040), but not after Holm adjustment (p = 0.120). Prevalence was lower on school than non-school days in children (56.7% vs 82.2%; based on three publications) and adolescents (50.6% vs 86.4%; both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). No robust sex differences were observed. Regional estimates varied substantially and require cautious interpretation because of extreme heterogeneity and uneven geographic representation. In conclusion, insufficient sleep appears especially common during adolescence and on school days, supporting strategies to improve sleep during the school week. papers.title: Folic Acid Oversupplementation Alters Global DNA Methylation and Circadian Clock Gene Expression in FaDu Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma Cells: An Exploratory Study.
papers.abstract: Folic acid (FA), the synthetic form of folate (vitamin B9), is a vitamin involved in one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis, and DNA methylation. Because folate metabolism influences methyl donor availability, FA availability may affect circadian clock gene regulation through methylation-related or other metabolic mechanisms in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). This exploratory study aims to determine whether FA oversupplementation influences cell viability and alters global DNA methylation, as well as the expression and methylation status of circadian clock genes in HNSCC cells. FaDu HNSCC cells were treated with 20 or 80 μM FA and compared with a no-added-FA (NF) reference condition. Cell viability was assessed using a CCK-8 assay after 48 and 72 h. For methylation and gene expression analyses, cells were synchronized with forskolin and treated with FA (20 or 80 μM) for 7 days. Global DNA methylation was measured using a 5-methylcytosine colorimetric assay. Following the NF and 80 μM FA treatment, cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) island methylation in the BMAL1 and PER2 promoters, RNA expression, and protein levels were analyzed by bisulfite conversion followed by Sanger sequencing, qPCR, and ELISA. FA treatment significantly reduced cell viability at 48 h (20 μM, p < 0.05; 80 μM, p < 0.01) and 72 h (both concentrations p < 0.01). Global DNA methylation was modestly reduced, reaching statistical significance only in the 80 μM FA group (p < 0.05). No qualitative differences were observed in the promoter methylation of the analyzed CpG regions of BMAL1 and PER2 following 80 μM FA treatment. However, BMAL1 and PER2 mRNA expressions were significantly increased (p < 0.05), while protein levels showed non-significant upward trends following 80 μM FA treatment. These exploratory findings suggest that the observed transcriptional changes are unlikely to be explained by methylation changes within the analyzed promoter regions of BMAL1 and PER2. The mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear and require further investigation.

papers.title: Circadian and Seasonal Patterns of Recorded Emergency Medical Service Workload by Diagnostic Category: A Two-Year Retrospective Analysis with Forecasting from Türkiye.
papers.abstract: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) demand varies across circadian, weekly, and seasonal timescales. This study is among the first such integrated analyses in the Turkish 112 EMS context. The primary objective of this study was to characterize circadian patterns in overall EMS case-record volume and across seven clinical groups, as well as hourly, weekly, and seasonal variation in diagnostic composition across eight categories. Secondary objectives were to estimate adjusted temporal associations and evaluate frozen transfer of aggregate daily forecasts from 2024 to the immediately subsequent 2025 holdout. This retrospective study analyzed 60,811 routinely collected EMS case-record rows from Karaman Province, Türkiye over 731 days in 2024-2025. Interaction, cosinor, and negative binomial (NB) models characterized temporal patterns; aggregate daily case-record volume was forecast using weekly Fourier terms with autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) errors trained on 2024 and frozen for 2025. The data represented provincial case-record workload, an operational proxy for population demand rather than a census of all inbound calls or unique patients. Case-record volume peaked at 21:00 and was lowest at 06:00; adjusted volume at 21:00 was 3.53-times that at 06:00 (95% CI, 3.28-3.81). Hourly diagnostic composition differed modestly (Cramér V = 0.061). Rhythmicity was detected in all seven clinical groups (all joint-test P values < 0.001), but low full-cell R2 values indicated substantial unexplained hour-date variation; acrophases ranged from 14:41 to 19:14 and relative amplitudes from 28.6% (Respiratory) to 67.9% (Trauma). Standardized Trauma share was higher in summer than winter (25.7% versus 18.1%), whereas Respiratory share was higher in winter than summer (9.7% versus 3.6%). Adjusted volume was higher on Monday than Saturday and higher in August than November (IRRs 1.11 and 1.23, respectively). In the frozen 2025 holdout, the selected model achieved mean absolute scaled error (MASE) = 0.722 and 95% prediction-interval coverage of 96.2%. Clinical-group rhythms and seasonal composition differences were observed. The frozen evaluation quantified aggregate daily forecast transfer only from 2024 to the immediately subsequent 2025 within one provincial series. Findings support local monitoring of recorded evening workload and seasonal diagnostic composition, particularly the higher Trauma share in summer and the higher Respiratory share in winter.

papers.title: Balancing Local and Global Dependencies in EEG Emotion Recognition via Multi-Scale Hybrid Attention.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based emotion recognition remains challenging due to the low signal-to-noise ratio, non-stationarity, strong inter-subject variability, and the distribution of affect-related information across multiple temporal resolutions. Although recent deep architectures have increasingly combined multi-scale local feature extraction with global dependency modeling, the adaptive integration of multi-scale representations before global encoding remains comparatively underexplored. To address this issue, we propose DSFConformer, an EEG emotion-recognition framework integrating multi-scale spatiotemporal convolution, Dynamic Sparse Feature Fusion (DSFF), and lightweight Transformer-based global modeling. The multi-scale encoder captures complementary local EEG dynamics at different temporal resolutions, while DSFF performs sample-adaptive feature reweighting and sparse suppression to reduce the influence of redundant or noise-sensitive responses. A Lite Transformer is subsequently employed to model global contextual dependencies with reduced computational cost. Experiments on the SEED dataset were conducted under complementary evaluation protocols. DSFConformer achieved an accuracy of 96.08% under chronological block-wise segment-level cross-validation. Under the stricter trial-wise protocol, it achieved 78.81% accuracy, statistically comparable to EEG-Conformer at 78.77%, with no significant paired difference. Ablation analyses further demonstrate that multi-scale convolution and DSFF provide the primary recognition-performance gains, whereas the Lite Transformer mainly improves computational efficiency while preserving comparable accuracy. Cross-session and leave-one-subject-out analyses further assess model robustness and generalization. Overall, the results indicate that adaptive sparse fusion of multi-scale EEG representations provides an effective approach for balancing local representation learning, noise-aware feature integration, and efficient global dependency modeling.

papers.title: Intelligent Wearable Respiratory Monitoring System Based on All-Electrospun Silver Nanowires/Graphene/Thermoplastic Polyurethane Strain Sensors.
papers.abstract: Respiration serves as a critical physiological indicator, with abnormalities in its patterns and rates closely associated with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, particularly sleep apnea syndrome (SAS). Wearable abdomen-mounted respiratory sensors offer a promising solution for long-term, comfortable, and noninvasive monitoring; however, the subtle mechanical deformations induced by respiration impose stringent requirements on sensor sensitivity and stability. Here, we report a versatile flexible strain sensor designed for comprehensive respiratory monitoring across diverse scenarios. This sensor adopts an all-fibrous and fully electrospun architecture composed of silver nanowires (AgNWs), graphene (GR), and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), which is fabricated through a dual-channel hybrid electrospinning strategy. The sensor exhibits dual-regime sensitivity. It delivers a stable and linear gauge factor (GF) of 133.3 in the low-strain range (0-40%), which is highly suitable for high-fidelity daily respiration monitoring. Meanwhile, a high GF is achieved in the high-strain region (>40%), enabling the accurate capture of vigorous physiological behaviors such as severe coughing and strenuous exercise. This multi-range sensitivity endows the sensor with high precision for subtle biological signals and reliable responsiveness to intense physiological events, along with outstanding flexibility, mechanical durability, and wearable comfort. Benefiting from the highly interpenetrated three-dimensional conductive network, the sensor enables precise detection of minute respiratory-induced deformations. Furthermore, an integrated respiratory monitoring system is developed, allowing accurate identification of different respiratory states through feature signal extraction and analysis. This work provides an efficient and scalable strategy for constructing high-performance dual-regime flexible strain sensors and demonstrates their strong potential for wearable respiratory health monitoring applications.

papers.title: Residual Sleep-Related Respiratory Events During Early Versus Long-Term NIV Follow-Up: Burden and Relationship with Gas Exchange.
papers.abstract: Background: A recent study published by our group demonstrated that patient-ventilator asynchrony (PVA) is independently associated with impaired gas exchange during long-term non-invasive ventilation (NIV). We aimed to determine whether the burden and phenotype of residual PVA vary according to disease category, NIV initiation context and follow-up timing, and whether the relationship between PVA and gas exchange differs according to follow-up timing. Methods: We performed a secondary analysis of 123 NIV-treated patients included in the primary study. PVA burden, upper-airway obstructive events and leaks were compared across disease categories and follow-up settings. Multivariable models for gas exchange outcomes were extended by introducing interaction terms between PVA burden and follow-up category. Patients underwent either long-term follow-up performed >3 months after NIV initiation (n = 74), early acute follow-up, i.e., after stabilization following NIV initiation in acute respiratory failure (n = 30), or early planned follow-up, i.e., within 3 months after NIV initiation in stable chronic respiratory failure (CRF) (n = 19). Results: Overall, leaks, upper airway obstructions (UAOs) and PVA burden did not significantly differ across disease categories, and neither leaks nor UAO differed across follow-up categories. In contrast, patients undergoing early follow-up after acute NIV initiation exhibited a significantly greater burden of residual PVA than those initiated in stable CRF, predominantly because of ineffective efforts. Within the subgroup of patients undergoing early follow-up, total PVA burden was more than doubled after acute NIV initiation (4.5% versus 1.5% of recording time; 6.2 versus 2.5 events·h-1). The association between PVA burden and post-NIV PaCO2 did not differ according to follow-up timing. Conversely, in an exploratory analysis limited to 40 patients, the relationship between PVA burden and nocturnal TcPCO2 was significantly attenuated during early compared with long-term follow-up (interaction β = -1.04, 95% CI -1.68 to -0.40; p = 0.003). However, this interaction was attenuated after adjustment for daytime PaCO2 (β = -0.55, 95% CI -1.12 to 0.03; p = 0.076). Stratified analyses demonstrated significant associations between PVA burden and both post-NIV PaCO2 (β = 0.38, p = 0.034) and nocturnal TcPCO2 (β = 0.80, p < 0.001) during routine long-term follow-up. Conclusions: Patients evaluated after acute NIV initiation exhibited the highest burden of residual PVA, predominantly ineffective efforts. However, PVA was independently associated with nocturnal hypercapnia primarily during established long-term NIV. These findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger prospectively monitored cohorts.

papers.title: Dynamic within-person associations between problematic social media use and sleep quality among university students: The mediating role of nomophobia and the moderating role of trait rumination.
papers.abstract: Problematic social media use (PSMU) and poor sleep quality are prevalent among university students. Although previous research has documented associations between PSMU and sleep problems, less is known about the short-term dynamic mechanisms underlying this relationship and the individual differences that may shape vulnerability. Drawing on intensive longitudinal data and dynamic structural equation modeling, this study examined a moderated mediation model in which nomophobia (i.e. anxiety or distress arising from being unable to access or use one's mobile phone) mediated the association between PSMU and poor sleep quality, with trait rumination examined as a moderator of this indirect association. A 21-day daily diary study was conducted with 228 Chinese university students. At the between-person level, higher PSMU was associated with greater nomophobia and poorer sleep quality. At the within-person level, increases in PSMU were prospectively associated with greater nomophobia, which subsequently predicted poorer sleep quality, supporting an indirect association through nomophobia. This indirect association was more pronounced among students with higher levels of trait rumination. By capturing dynamic day-to-day processes, these findings extend current understanding of how PSMU may contribute to poorer sleep during emerging adulthood and highlight nomophobia and rumination as potential targets for interventions aimed at promoting healthier digital habits and sleep.

papers.title: Percussive Vibration Therapy as an Adjunct to Conventional Physiotherapy in Chronic Non-Specific Low Back Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hand-held percussive vibration therapy (PVT) is widely used in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, yet its incremental benefit beyond an active physiotherapy program for chronic non-specific low back pain (CNLBP) is unclear. We investigated whether PVT added to conventional physiotherapy (CPT) improves disability, sleep quality, and pain. Methods: This single-center, parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized trial enrolled 50 adults aged 18-65 years with CNLBP and baseline visual analogue scale (VAS) pain ≥4/10. Participants were allocated equally to PVT + CPT or CPT alone and attended three sessions weekly for eight weeks. The Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) was the primary outcome; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and VAS scores were secondary outcomes. Week-8 scores were analyzed with baseline-adjusted ANCOVA using HC3 robust standard errors. Results: Follow-up data were complete for all participants. The adjusted ODI score at week 8 was 2.59 points higher with PVT + CPT than with CPT (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47 to 4.71; p = 0.017), a statistically significant difference in favor of CPT. PSQI scores did not differ between groups (adjusted difference, 0.25; 95% CI, -0.40 to 0.90; p = 0.451). VAS scores were lower with PVT + CPT (adjusted difference, -1.15; 95% CI, -1.45 to -0.85; p < 0.001). Conclusions: PVT did not provide an additional benefit for disability and did not improve sleep quality when added to CPT. The pain difference was a secondary, exploratory finding of uncertain clinical relevance.

papers.title: Cross-species multi-omics integration reveals lung alterations in acute kidney injury across mouse, pig, and human airway organoid models
papers.abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently associated with the development of distant acute lung injury (ALI); however, its broader clinical impact and the underlying temporal molecular mechanics remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We used aggregate deidentified Epic Cosmos data to describe all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay (LOS) in an AKI cohort (13,815,092 patients; 2016-2025) and a subgroup with subsequent lung injury (AKI-lung). Mechanistically, we integrated matched RNA-seq and proteomics from a hyper-acute pig model (4 h reperfusion), an established mouse model (24 h reperfusion), and primary lung organoids exposed to mtDAMP-conditioned media, using MOFA+, PROGENy, decoupleR/CollecTRI, and DIABLO. Candidates were validated in primary human donor lungs obtained from LifeLink, separated into Control (< 1.3 mg/dL, n = 4) and Clinical AKI ([≥] 1.3 mg/dL, n = 3) groups based on admission blood creatinine level. Results: The AKI-lung subgroup had higher observed mortality than the overall AKI cohort (36.67% vs. 25.45%, p < 0.001). Mean hospital LOS was 11.3 versus 6.9 days in the reported AKI-lung and AKI alone queries, respectively (unadjusted p < 0.001). Multi-omics analyses cross-species indicated a temporal shift in proteogenomic coupling. In the hyper-acute pig model, we observed a largely post-translational response (r = -0.06), including ciliary breakdown and metabolic changes associated with PDHA1 protein depletion (Log2FC = -1.53), with minimal transcript level changes. The established mouse model showed a coordinated transcriptional inflammatory response (r = 0.316), characterized by PI3K/Akt pathway activation and downregulation of vascular and immune regulators (Aplnr, Cd74). Human lung organoids exhibited transcriptional downregulation of tissue remodeling genes and persistent ATF6/ATF4-associated ER stress, consistent with a reparative phase under proteostatic strain. Unsupervised MOFA+ revealed conserved cross-species axes (Factors 6 and 7) linked to vascular repair and hemostasis. Upstream regulon analysis identified the endothelial integrity regulators, including FOXF1. Most importantly, targeted validation in primary human donor lungs confirmed a statistically significant, selective down-regulation of the core circadian regulator circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) transcript (p < 0.05), independent of donor age, sex, race. Conclusions: Aggregate clinical findings suggest an association between lung injury following AKI and worse outcome. Kidney-Lung crosstalk initiates as hyper-acute post-translational microvascular breakdown in swine and rapidly transitions into localized uncoupling of cell-autonomous pulmonary circadian machinery (CLOCK) in clinical human AKI, offering human-validated targets to intercept distant organ failure.

papers.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of antihistamines, increased antihistamine dosing, and antihistamine adjuncts for chronic urticaria: a systematic review, dose-response, and network meta-analysis of randomized trials.
papers.abstract: Chronic urticaria is a common immune-mediated condition characterized by wheals (itch and hives), angioedema, or both, lasting for greater than six weeks. It is managed with H1 antihistamines as the first-line therapy. Fundamental unresolved questions remain regarding the comparative benefits and harms of antihistamines and their adjuncts, and of H1 antihistamine dose-escalation. To analyze the comparative benefits and harms of antihistamines and their adjuncts (H2 blockers or montelukast), and of H1 antihistamine dose-escalation. As part of updating the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology and American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology Joint Task Force on Practice Parameters Chronic Urticaria guidelines, we searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and regulatory databases from inception to March 17, 2025, for randomized trials addressing antihistamines or their adjuncts for chronic urticaria. Paired reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Random effects network and dose-response meta-analyses addressed urticaria activity (composed of itch and wheal scores), angioedema activity, urticaria-related quality of life, and harms including sedation. The GRADE approach informed certainty of evidence ratings. CRD42022367280. 211 trials (22,187 participants) evaluated 55 unique treatments. Bilastine, desloratadine, fexofenadine, and levocetirizine are among the most effective in improving overall urticaria activity, urticaria-related quality of life, and sleep disturbance. Cetirizine and loratadine are among the most effective in reducing overall urticaria activity and its subcomponents, with cetirizine also among the most effective in improving urticaria-related quality of life. Escalating from a single to quadruple daily dose may yield diminishing additional benefit. Second-generation agents as a class may be more effective than first-generation agents in improving urticaria activity and sleep disturbance. Sedation risk likely increases with higher doses, with first-generation agents (e.g., diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) and doxepin among the most sedating; cetirizine, ketotifen, levocetirizine, and rupatadine among the intermediate sedating; and bepotastine, bilastine, desloratadine, ebastine, fexofenadine, and loratadine among the least sedating. Adding montelukast (moderate certainty) or an H2 blocker (very low certainty) to a second-generation agent may further reduce urticaria activity. For chronic urticaria, second-generation agents differ in their efficacy and safety. First-generation agents are less beneficial and more harmful. Escalating to higher daily doses may provide additional benefits but likely increases sedation.
